title: The Atlantic jigsaw
hook: South America and Africa look like they fit. Close the ocean and test it.

knows: that South America and Africa have matching-looking coasts
doesNotKnow: that the match holds up as geometry when one continent is turned as a rigid piece

misconception: The coast match is a coincidence people over-read; continents have always been where they are.
objective: The learner can describe that turning South America as one rigid piece about a single pole closes it against Africa, with Brazil's bulge in the Gulf of Guinea, and that this fit is evidence the continents were joined.

claims.text: On the stage, South America is turned as one solid piece 57° about a single point in the North Atlantic (44°N, 30.6°W), and its coast closes against Africa's.
claims.source: Bullard, E., Everett, J. E. and Smith, A. G. (1965), The fit of the continents around the Atlantic, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 258(1088): 41-51 (South America to Africa: pole 44.0 N, 30.6 W, rotation 57.0 degrees, fitted at the 500-fathom isobath). Parameters from the brief and builder recall; not opened (network blocked). It is a best fit of margins, not a plate-motion history. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): RE-OPENED in pass 9: this was marked verified but its source says the parameters came from builder recall and the paper was not opened. Bullard, Everett and Smith (1965), Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 258: 41-51, is unreachable (royalsocietypublishing.org 403); a web search found no secondary source quoting 44.0 N, 30.6 W, 57.0 degrees. Needs a human source check of the paper's table. Note: c4 (500-fathom contour) rests on the same unopened paper. | v2 (2026-10-14): claim text rewritten to match the revised stage; previous verification void, needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Pass 21: still not opened (royalsocietypublishing, geologie.ens.fr OCR copy and Morgan 1968 PDF all blocked to fetch). Web-search extracts: an OCR of the paper lists fit 9 (500 fm) as '44.0 30.6 57.0', and Morgan (1968) cites Bullard et al. for a 44.0 N, 30.6 W pole; but Virtual Explorer (2007) lists Bullard et al. (1965) as 42.9, -30.1, 57.1 and gives 44/-30.6/57 to Smith and Hallam (1970). The learner sentence depends on the unopened table and secondary sources conflict, so disputed. To clear: a human opens Table 1 (fit 9) in Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 258: 41-51 (copy at geologie.ens.fr/50years_plate_tectonics/phil-trans-r-soc-lond-a.pdf). · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Still disputed, unchanged since pass 21 (claim and stage not edited). The source host (geologie.ens.fr) does not resolve from this sandbox, so Table 1 of Bullard, Everett and Smith (1965) is still unopened. To clear: a human opens Table 1, fit 9. | REVISED v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): v3 drops the attribution 'which is the fit Bullard, Everett and Smith published in 1965', because Table 1 of that paper could not be opened and secondary sources disagree on the pole (44.0/30.6/57.0 vs 42.9/30.1/57.1). The sentence now says only what the stage does: the angle and the pole are the lesson's model parameters (Demo.tsx POLE, ANGLE), and the closing is the stage check behind c2 and c3. The learner no longer sees the paper or a claim that these are published values. Unverified.

claims.text: Brazil's eastern bulge lands in the Gulf of Guinea, near Nigeria and Cameroon.
claims.source: Rodrigues rotation of (34.8 W, 7.1 S) by +57 degrees about (44 N, 30.6 W) gives 7.27 E, 4.98 N; the nearest 1:110m African outline vertex is Nigeria's, 61 km away (artifacts/scratch/w1-jigsaw.mjs). The rotation sense (+57) is the one that brings South America to Africa; -57 sends it to the Pacific.

claims.text: With today's coarse coastlines the coasts close up with only small gaps and overlaps; the fit is rough.
claims.source: 1,551 one-degree sample points inside the South American shapes: 3 land inside an African country after the turn; Brazil's east-coast vertices end a mean 148 km (max 302 km) from the nearest African vertex (w1-jigsaw.mjs). No km figure is shown to the learner.

claims.text: Published fits of these coasts use the edge of the continental shelf, not today's shoreline.
claims.source: Bullard et al. (1965) fitted the 500-fathom (about 900 m) contour. | REVISED v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): reveal reworded from 'their fit used' to 'published fits use the edge of the continental shelf', because the reveal no longer names Bullard et al.. Unverified.

claims.text: A rotation on the sphere keeps South America's size and shape; only its place changes.
claims.source: Rotations of the sphere are isometries. Demo.tsx applies one rotation to every vertex (kit mapFeature).

claims.text: The South Atlantic began opening roughly 130 million years ago.
claims.source: Frisch, Meschede and Blakey (2011), Plate Tectonics, Springer: South Atlantic rifting and opening in the Early Cretaceous, about 140-120 Ma. Not opened by the builder. | v2: sentence no longer shown to learners; withdrawn.

claims.text: Two coasts this far apart rarely match by chance; the fit is evidence the continents were once joined.
claims.source: Interpretive claim; Bullard et al. (1965) and standard plate-tectonics texts present the fit as evidence for continental drift. The lesson does not claim the fit alone proves it.

recall.question: When South America is turned back against Africa, Brazil's eastern bulge sits:
options: In the Gulf of Guinea, under West Africa
recall.why: Turned as one rigid piece about a single pole, the bulge tucks under West Africa's coast into the Gulf of Guinea.
